content: Comforting behaviors such as the use of pacifiers, blankets, and finger or thumb sucking are common in infants and young children. These behaviors, collectively referred to as non-nutritive sucking habits (NNSHs), typically diminish as children grow older, either naturally or with guidance from parents or caregivers. However, if these habits persist during the development of permanent teeth, they can contribute to or cause malocclusion, which is an abnormal alignment of the teeth or bite. Various methods have been employed to help children stop NNSHs. These include providing advice, removing the comforting object, using orthodontic appliances to disrupt the habit, applying aversive-tasting substances to the fingers, or employing behavior modification techniques. Some of these interventions are easier to implement and less distressing for the child and their parents, while others may be more suitable for specific types of habits. The primary goal of this review was to assess the effectiveness of different interventions for stopping NNSHs in children. Secondary objectives included identifying which interventions work the fastest, are the most effective, and cause the least discomfort or psychological distress for the child and their caregivers. Additionally, the review aimed to evaluate the impact of these interventions on dental outcomes, such as reducing anterior open bite, overjet, and correcting posterior crossbite, as well as their cost-effectiveness. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, up to October 8, 2014. They also searched clinical trial registries and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving children with NNSHs were included if they compared one intervention to another or to a no-intervention control group. The primary outcome of interest was the cessation of the habit. Six trials involving 252 children (aged 2.5 to 18 years) were included in the review, although follow-up data were available for only 246 children. All studies focused on digit sucking as the NNSH. Five studies compared one or more interventions to a no-treatment or waiting list control group, while one study directly compared two active interventions. The studies were generally of low quality, with significant methodological and reporting limitations, small sample sizes (20 to 38 participants per study), and follow-up periods ranging from 1 to 36 months. Short-term outcomes were defined as those observed within one year post-intervention, while long-term outcomes were observed at one year or more post-intervention. Two trials evaluated the use of orthodontic appliances (palatal cribs or a combination of palatal cribs and arches) compared to no treatment. Both trials were at high risk of bias. The use of orthodontic appliances was more effective than no treatment in stopping digit sucking in both the short term (risk ratio [RR] 6.53, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.67 to 25.53; 2 trials, 70 participants) and the long term (RR 5.81, 95% CI 1.49 to 22.66; 1 trial, 37 participants). When combined with psychological interventions, orthodontic appliances also showed a higher likelihood of cessation (RR 6.36, 95% CI 0.97 to 41.96; 1 trial, 32 participants). Two trials (78 participants) assessed psychological interventions, such as positive reinforcement (alone or combined with gaining the child’s cooperation) or negative reinforcement, compared to no treatment. These trials were also at high risk of bias. Pooled data showed a statistically significant benefit of psychological interventions in the short term (RR 6.16, 95% CI 1.18 to 32.10; I² = 0%). One study with 57 participants reported long-term outcomes and found a statistically significant benefit of psychological interventions for habit cessation (RR 6.25, 95% CI 1.65 to 23.65). Only one trial directly compared two active interventions, involving 22 participants. This study found that the palatal crib was more effective than the palatal arch in stopping the habit (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.59). The authors concluded that there is low-quality evidence suggesting that orthodontic appliances (palatal cribs and palatal arches) and psychological interventions (positive and negative reinforcement) are effective in promoting the cessation of NNSHs in children. There is very low-quality evidence indicating that palatal cribs may be more effective than palatal arches. The review highlights the need for high-quality trials to evaluate interventions for stopping NNSHs and calls for a standardized approach to reporting outcomes in such studies.
